note: Units of the panel for the research chat: one short English text per risk, alert, indicator, term, scene, verdict and the week's feed. Concepts are not here — they live in the 'concepts' namespace.

units.title: A very strong El Niño is under way
units.text: A very strong El Niño is under way Water in the key patch of the Pacific is 2.9 degrees warmer than normal. The threshold for a “very strong” event is two degrees. This is not a forecast, it is already measured, and no year since 1982 was this warm on these dates. Niño 3.4 by the NOAA weekly index +2.9 °C on 2026-09-09; daily OISST +2.96. Among all years since 1982 for the same 30 days: rank 1. What to watch: the NOAA weekly index; the official ONI is now +1.80 (JJA), the “very strong” category starts at +2.0 on the three-month average

units.title: The fuel is at its record and has not started to burn
units.text: The fuel is at its record and has not started to burn The heat that will surface later is already piled up under the equator, and it is at a record for the whole series. This is measured, not forecast: the surface has not yet shown what is already stored below. While the gauge is not falling, the event has something to grow on. Warm water volume 3.24·10¹⁴ m³, 100 % of the highest value of the series since 1980; the latest month, 2026-07, is itself the peak. On our own data this gauge leads the surface index by 6 months. What to watch: the monthly PMEL update: the first clear fall of the volume is the earliest honest sign that the peak is near

units.title: Water +11.3 °C above normal is sitting at 100 m under 125°W
units.text: Water +11.3 °C above normal is sitting at 100 m under 125°W This is the heat that has not surfaced yet. It is measured directly by the moorings, and it is what makes 'the event has room to grow' a statement about the present rather than about the past events. TAO mooring 125°W, five-day mean to 2026-09-01 (16 days old on this run), against the mooring's own 1991–2020 norm. The mooring's own maximum before this event was +12.9 °C at 140 m on 1997-11-18. The 20 °C isotherm is at 166.7 m in the west and 130.2 m in the east. What to watch: the warm anomaly moving east along the moorings and rising toward the surface; the east D20 shallowing again would mean the wave has passed

units.title: The event has room to grow: the fuel is charged and the analogues peaked in winter
units.text: The event has room to grow: the fuel is charged and the analogues peaked in winter Every past event of this strength peaked in winter, between mid-November and early February. It is the end of summer now, so two or three more months of growth are likely. How much higher cannot be said: we are already above anything the ocean has shown at this time of year, and past events are no guide here. The real question is when the growth stops. Past analogues peaked in November to early February. Adding their gain from the same date gives +3.3 … +4.6 °C, above the record of the series +3.02. What to watch: if the weekly Niño 3.4 stops rising before November, the event has reached its plateau earlier than the analogues

units.title: The eastern Pacific is heating, off the coast of South America
units.text: The eastern Pacific is heating, off the coast of South America There are two kinds of El Niño: one heats the middle of the ocean, the other the east, off Peru and Ecuador. This is the second kind, the harshest in its consequences: 1982 and 1997 were like this. Such events brought downpours and floods to the coast of South America and droughts to Indonesia and Australia. Niño 1+2 +4.5, Niño 4 +0.9: difference +3.6 °C. What to watch: the difference staying above 1 °C through September and October

units.title: The world ocean is warmer every day than it has ever been on that day
units.text: The world ocean is warmer every day than it has ever been on that day On each of the last 30 days the ocean, averaged over the planet, was warmer than on the same day of any year since 1982. Not one hot day, but an unbroken stretch. 30 record days out of the last 30, a run of 30 days in a row; 120 of 259 days this year. What to watch: the first day below the record without a change of season is the first sign of a turn

units.title: Niño 3.4: not a spike but a new level
units.text: Niño 3.4: not a spike but a new level The series did not jump and come back; it rose and stayed. The gauge that accumulates the excess over the spring level crossed its threshold 98 days ago and has only grown since. accumulated shift +147 against a threshold of 5; first over the threshold 98 days ago What to watch: if the accumulated gauge starts to fall, the regime is letting go

units.title: Some forecast models are already below reality
units.text: Some forecast models are already below reality Of 26 models, 15 have already fallen behind what the ocean showed this week. They are not “wrong about the future”; they are not keeping up with the present. Their winter forecasts are most likely too low. 15 of 26 models gave less for ASO than the already reached +2.9 °C: BCC_RZDM, CPC MRKOV, CS-IRI-MM, CSU CLIPR, IAP-NN, IOCAS ICM and others. Model mean +2.79, spread +1.60…+3.75. What to watch: the next IRI issue: how many models catch up

units.title: The year after the peak: 2027 is likely to be warmer than 2026
units.text: The year after the peak: 2027 is likely to be warmer than 2026 El Niño releases the ocean's heat into the air with a lag of a few months, so the calendar year that follows the peak is usually the warmer one. That is why 1998, 2016 and 2024 each became the warmest year measured up to that point. On the same arithmetic, next year is the one to plan for, not this one. In 1982→1983 +0.19 °C, 1997→1998 +0.19 °C, 2015→2016 +0.18 °C, 2023→2024 +0.12 °C (annual land+ocean mean, ERA5); warmer in 4 of 4 analogues, median +0.19. What to watch: annual land+ocean mean once the peak passes; the first months of next year already carry the signal

units.title: The air is answering the ocean, so the event can travel
units.text: The air is answering the ocean, so the event can travel El Niño is not a warm patch of water, it is a coupling: the water heats, the trade winds give way, the cloud tower moves east, and only then does the event reach harvests on the other side of the planet. All three are in place now, which is why the regional impacts on this page are worth taking seriously. Southern Oscillation Index -1.1, convection at the date line -1.0 standard deviations, trade wind in the west -2.0. 3 of 3 atmospheric signs are in place. What to watch: the same three: if the winds return and the convection moves back west, the event stays in the ocean and the teleconnections fade

units.title: The upper 300 m of the central and eastern Pacific hold +2.51 °C of extra heat
units.text: The upper 300 m of the central and eastern Pacific hold +2.51 °C of extra heat The CPC calls this the upper-ocean heat content index and watches it as the leading sign of where the surface goes next. One degree across that band is already a large charge; this is 2.5. GODAS reanalysis, 2026-07: mean temperature anomaly of 0–300 m across 180–100°W, our climatology; the reanalysis' warmest point is 9.19 °C at 75.0 m, 104.5°W. What to watch: the index in the next monthly GODAS; the moorings above show it a month earlier

units.title: A westerly wind burst is under way over the western Pacific
units.text: A westerly wind burst is under way over the western Pacific The trade winds have given way for a week or more. Each burst pushes warm water down and east; the Kelvin wave it launches reaches the American coast in two to three months and lifts the event another step. Since 2026-09-06: 6 days at or above the threshold of 4.11 m/s, peak anomaly 6.46 m/s (ERA5 10 m wind, six points 130°E–180°). What to watch: the burst ending; the eastern moorings' 20 °C isotherm deepening two to three months from now

units.title: The models keep revising the forecast upward, issue after issue
units.text: The models keep revising the forecast upward, issue after issue When almost all models move their forecast in the same direction, the event is outrunning them. The shift itself is a signal: the next issue will probably be higher again. Since the Jul 2026 issue 25 of 25 models raised their peak, 0 lowered it; combined peak +2.95 → +3.28 °C; the combined peak has risen in 11 consecutive issues. What to watch: the IRI issue around the 19th

units.title: A La Niña usually follows within a year or two
units.text: A La Niña usually follows within a year or two The ocean does not simply return to normal: after a strong El Niño it usually swings the other way. A La Niña flips the map of impacts, so the regions that are dry now tend to be wet then, and the grain exporters that had a good year tend to have a bad one. Planning that only covers this winter misses the swing. After the analogues the ONI fell to 1982: -1.06, 1997: -1.53, 2015: -0.76, 2023: -0.61; it crossed the La Niña threshold of −0.5 in 4 of 4 cases. What to watch: the ONI trend after the peak; a fall of 0.3 or more per month is the usual signature of the swing

units.title: Global temperature in 2027 is likely to run above 2026; regional impacts follow their own lags
units.text: Global temperature in 2027 is likely to run above 2026; regional impacts follow their own lags The dashboard measures the ocean today, but people meet an El Niño through harvests, water and prices, and those arrive with a delay of six to eighteen months. The plans that matter are for next year: import contracts, reserves, water rationing, insurance. Land+ocean is +0.57 °C above trend now, while the ocean heat that drives it is still rising; in the analogues the air-temperature records, the harvest failures and the price effects all came in the year after the onset. What to watch: the first harvests after the peak season and the food price index six to twelve months from the onset

units.title: The atmosphere is still catching up: three floors follow the ocean with a 3-month delay
units.text: The atmosphere is still catching up: three floors follow the ocean with a 3-month delay The ocean heats the air, not the other way round, and the air takes months to answer. That is why the warmest months of the whole record usually arrive AFTER the peak of an El Niño, not during it — and why the year that follows this one is the one to watch. Satellite lower troposphere in the tropics +0.90 °C; on our own data this layer follows Niño 3.4 with a delay of 3 months (correlation 0.69). What to watch: the monthly satellite layers: the tropics react first, the global mean follows

units.title: The ocean holds more heat than ever measured (0–2000 m)
units.text: The ocean holds more heat than ever measured (0–2000 m) This is the reservoir the event draws on and returns to. A record reservoir means the statistical forecasts, trained on a cooler ocean, are reading a different system than the one they learned. 33.97 × 10²² J in 2026 Q1, a record of the series since 2005; up 11.2 in ten years. What to watch: the next quarterly NCEI update; whether the 0–2000 m series keeps rising through the event

Weight 2 of 5: an input for aquaculture and poultry feed; small in the human diet but the most direct El Niño price signal. Also: +22 % since the event began. Peru: the anchoveta leaves the warm water. This is the most direct price signal of an El Niño.

units.title: El Niño
units.text: El Niño A periodic warming of the water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific. It comes every 2 to 7 years, lasts about a year, and usually peaks in the northern-hemisphere winter. It changes the weather on half the planet: droughts in Australia, Indonesia and southern Africa, downpours in Peru and East Africa, a weak monsoon in India. NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ENSO FAQ

units.title: La Niña
units.text: La Niña The opposite phase: water in the same patches is colder than normal. The weather effects are roughly mirrored. A strong El Niño is often followed by La Niña; that is the next story the watchdog will follow once the event turns. NOAA CPC

units.title: Niño 4
units.text: Niño 4 The central-western part, 160°E to 150°W. The difference “Niño 1+2 minus Niño 4” shows the type of the event: eastern (warm edge by the Americas) or central. NOAA CPC

units.title: Niño 3.4
units.text: Niño 3.4 A patch of the Pacific between 5°S and 5°N, 170°W to 120°W. The temperature anomaly of its water is the main measure of El Niño. All thresholds, weak / moderate / strong / very strong, are set on Niño 3.4: +0.5 / +1.0 / +1.5 / +2.0 °C. NOAA CPC, weekly indices wksst9120

units.title: Niño 3
units.text: Niño 3 The eastern part of the equatorial band, 150°W to 90°W. The alert fires when Niño 3 goes above anything the weekly series has measured, as it did in this event: the eastern half of the band is where an eastern-type El Niño shows first. NOAA CPC

units.title: Niño 1+2
units.text: Niño 1+2 The coastal patch off Peru and Ecuador (0 to 10°S, 90 to 80°W). The easternmost of the four. It warms first in an eastern-type event. When Niño 1+2 cools fast while Niño 3.4 is still warm, the coastal phase is ending. NOAA CPC

units.title: ONI
units.text: ONI The Oceanic Niño Index, NOAA's official measure: the Niño 3.4 anomaly averaged over three consecutive months, from ERSST monthly data. An event is officially very strong when ONI ≥ +2.0. A three-month mean is always lower and later than the weekly value, so ONI catches up. NOAA CPC, oni.ascii.txt

units.title: SOI
units.text: SOI The Southern Oscillation Index: the pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin. The atmospheric side of the same phenomenon. A negative SOI confirms El Niño from the atmosphere; if the ocean is warm but SOI does not fall, the event has not “caught”. NOAA CPC, data/indices/soi

units.title: Eastern and central type
units.text: Eastern and central type Eastern (canonical): the warmest water is off the coast of South America. Central (Modoki): the focus is shifted towards the date line. Their consequences differ: the eastern type hits Peru and Ecuador harder with rain and gives the more classic droughts in Australia and Indonesia. Ashok et al., 2007; NOAA CPC

units.title: Anomaly and the 1991–2020 climatology
units.text: Anomaly and the 1991–2020 climatology An anomaly is the departure from the norm for the same day of the year. The norm (climatology) is the 1991–2020 mean, taken from the source files themselves. “+2.6 °C” here always means “2.6 degrees warmer than usual for this date”, not an absolute temperature. climatereanalyzer.org, climatology fields in the JSON

units.title: Trend and “above trend”
units.text: Trend and “above trend” The ocean warms year on year. “Above trend” is the anomaly after subtracting the linear warming across years. Without this any recent year beats the old ones through warming rather than through the event. Every “this year against others” comparison is made above trend. computed in tools/enso/watch.py

units.title: Rank
units.text: Rank The position of the current value among the same calendar days of all years in the series. “1 of 45” means above all of them. A rank is more honest than a mean: it says “this has not happened” without assumptions about the distribution. computed in tools/enso/watch.py

units.title: Percentile
units.text: Percentile “98th percentile” means it happens in only 2 % of years at this time of year. Slope and noise are compared with the same windows of the same season, so a percentile means “unusual for this time of year”, not “unusual in general”. computed in tools/enso/watch.py

units.title: CUSUM
units.text: CUSUM A gauge that accumulates excess: every day the sum grows by how far the series is above the level at the start of the window, in units of the series' spread. Threshold 5. It catches “rose and stayed” rather than a spike. When CUSUM turns down, the regime is letting go earlier than a mean would show. Page, 1954; computed in tools/enso/watch.py, 180-day window

units.title: Analogue forecast
units.text: Analogue forecast To today's level we add the change of every past year over the same two weeks. The result is a distribution of outcomes. No climate model: only “how the series moved at this time of year before”. Honest and explainable; horizon 14 days. computed in tools/enso/watch.py

units.title: p10 / p50 / p90
units.text: p10 / p50 / p90 Three marks of a distribution: below p10 happens in 10 % of cases, p50 is the middle, above p90 in 10 %. Read it as “from … to …, most likely around p50”. computed in tools/enso/watch.py

units.title: IRI model plume
units.text: IRI model plume A digest of Niño 3.4 forecasts from two dozen centres worldwide for nine seasons ahead, published by IRI (Columbia University) around the 19th of every month. The only open place where the forecasts of all models stand side by side. We parse the SVG figure, accuracy ±0.05 °C. iri.columbia.edu, ENSO forecast plume

units.title: Dynamical and statistical models
units.text: Dynamical and statistical models Dynamical models compute the physics of ocean and atmosphere (ECMWF, NASA, UKMO…). Statistical ones look for patterns in past data, neural networks included. In strong events the statistical models usually fall behind first: their history simply contains no such levels. IRI, plume description

units.title: Forecast lead
units.text: Forecast lead How many months before the target season the forecast was made. Lead 1 is one month ahead, lead 6 half a year. A model that errs at lead 6 is normal; at lead 1 it is not. The “keeping up / lagging” assessment looks at leads 1 to 3. IRI

units.title: Three-letter seasons
units.text: Three-letter seasons ASO is August-September-October, NDJ is November-December-January, and so on: three months by their first letters. Both ONI and the forecasts are computed on rolling three-month windows; that damps the monthly noise. NOAA CPC

units.title: Teleconnection
units.text: Teleconnection A stable statistical link between the state of the Pacific and the weather in a distant region, through a rearrangement of the atmospheric circulation. Teleconnections are typical, not guaranteed: the page must say “usually”, never “will”. NOAA CPC, maps of typical impacts

units.title: Net food importer
units.text: Net food importer A country that brings in more food than it sends out. Dependence is measured by the share of imports in grain consumption. For a net importer El Niño strikes not through its own harvest but through prices and availability on the world market. FAO, World Bank

units.title: FAO Food Price Index
units.text: FAO Food Price Index A monthly index of world food prices (2014–16 = 100) and five groups: cereals, oils, meat, dairy, sugar. The only live food series available without registration. Lag: one month. fao.org, Food Price Index

units.title: Risk index 0–100
units.text: Risk index 0–100 Two scales in one. 0 to 90 is a saturating sum of risk levels 1 to 5: 90·(1 − exp(−Σ level^1.5 / 25)), so a full board of level-5 risks reaches 90 and never more. The last ten points are a reserve for readings that go past the record itself: they open only when a series is above its own historical maximum for that calendar day, is moving fast against its own history of 14-day slopes, and does both on several systems at once. 90 means “stronger than anything we have on record”, not “the end”; 100 is kept for something unprecedented arriving fast. This is our scale, not an official one. computed in tools/enso/watch.py

units.title: OISST v2.1
units.text: OISST v2.1 NOAA's daily sea-surface temperature from satellites and buoys, since 1981, on a 0.25° grid. The final grid lags by two to three weeks; the preliminary grid (OISST NRT, see that entry) is one day behind and is spliced onto the long series, so the daily boxes on this panel are one day old. The last days are marked preliminary and re-pulled until the final values arrive. climatereanalyzer.org → NOAA OISST

units.title: ERA5
units.text: ERA5 The ECMWF reanalysis: air temperature at 2 m over land and ocean, since 1940. It gives “land+ocean”, what people feel as heat, as opposed to the temperature of the water. climatereanalyzer.org → ECMWF ERA5

units.title: NOAA weekly
units.text: NOAA weekly Anomalies of the four Niño regions for the week centred on Wednesday, published by NOAA CPC on Mondays. The reference the forecast models are judged against and the index the strength rule uses; fresher than the final daily grid, a few days older than the preliminary one. Where the two disagree, the panel shows both. NOAA CPC, wksst9120.for

units.title: The turning-point watchdog
units.text: The turning-point watchdog A set of rules, not a model: above the historical maximum, a reversal of growth at a high level, a fall of 0.3 or more in two weeks, ONI crossing +2.0, reality above every model: SHOUT; everything else: WATCH. The subsurface alert follows the same idea: WATCH from +5 °C at a mooring, SHOUT only above that mooring's own maximum before this event. One hand-set exception remains: the FAO index at a five-year high is SHOUT. Price and model alerts have their own rules, described on the Food and Models tabs. The rules are checkable: each compares a fresh number with the record of the series, the previous snapshot, or the same season in history. The model does not invent them. tools/enso/alerts.py

units.title: Model summary
units.text: Model summary DeepSeek receives only the digest of the block's facts, numbers, ranks and alerts, and answers in strict JSON. Not one number from outside. The summary is an interpretation, not a source: every number in it must be in the digest. Without a key the page shows a rule-based digest, marked as such. tools/enso/summary.py

units.title: Warm water volume
units.text: Warm water volume The volume of water warmer than 20 °C in the upper 300 m of the equatorial Pacific, between 120°E and 80°W. Measured by moored buoys and floats, published monthly by NOAA PMEL. It is the fuel gauge of an El Nino: the heat piles up below the surface before it shows up on top. On our own series it leads the surface index by about half a year, so it answers the question the models can only guess at - whether the event still has something to grow on. NOAA PMEL / TAO-TRITON

units.title: Upper 300 m temperature
units.text: Upper 300 m temperature The average temperature anomaly of the top 300 metres of the equatorial Pacific. The same stored heat as the warm water volume, expressed as a temperature instead of a volume. Easier to compare with the surface numbers on the rest of this panel: both are in degrees. NOAA PMEL / TAO-TRITON

units.title: Outgoing longwave radiation
units.text: Outgoing longwave radiation How much heat the planet radiates to space over a given patch of ocean, here 5N-5S, 160E-160W. Tall clouds are cold on top, so they radiate less: a NEGATIVE anomaly means the cloud tower has moved in. This is where the ocean hands the event over to the atmosphere. When convection shifts to the date line, the jet streams shift with it, and that is what carries El Nino to harvests on the other side of the planet. NOAA CPC

units.title: Trade wind at 850 hPa
units.text: Trade wind at 850 hPa The east-west wind at about 1.5 km altitude, averaged over 5N-5S in three longitude bands. Normally it blows from the east; a negative anomaly means the trades have weakened or reversed to westerlies. Weakened trades let the warm pool slide east and trigger the Kelvin waves that carry it. It is both a symptom of the event and one of its engines. NOAA CPC

units.title: Coupling
units.text: Coupling Whether the atmosphere is answering the ocean. We count three signs: pressure across the Pacific (SOI), convection at the date line (OLR) and the trade winds - each in standard deviations, each called in place below -0.5. A warm patch of water with no atmospheric response stays a warm patch of water. The distant impacts - drought, floods, harvests - travel through the air, not through the sea. our own rule over NOAA CPC series

units.title: Satellite layers
units.text: Satellite layers Temperature of four floors of the atmosphere measured from satellites: lower troposphere, mid troposphere, tropopause and lower stratosphere (UAH v6.1, monthly). The ocean heats the air with a delay, and the delay is measured here against our own Nino 3.4 series rather than taken from a textbook. It explains why the warmest months of the record tend to arrive after the peak of an El Nino, not during it. UAH, University of Alabama in Huntsville

units.title: Pink Sheet
units.text: Pink Sheet The World Bank's monthly table of world commodity prices - grains, oils, sugar, fertilisers, energy - free and without registration. The FAO index is one number for all food. El Nino does not hit food in general: it hits palm oil, rice and fishmeal by name, each through its own country and its own season. World Bank

units.title: NOAA CPC
units.text: NOAA CPC The Climate Prediction Center of the American weather service. It publishes the weekly Nino indices, the official ONI, the Southern Oscillation Index and the tropical wind and convection indices. Most of the numbers on this panel that are not our own arithmetic come from here. It is the reference source for ENSO: when forecasters argue, they argue about CPC data. NOAA Climate Prediction Center

units.title: NOAA PMEL / TAO
units.text: NOAA PMEL / TAO The Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory and its array of moored buoys along the equator, TAO/TRITON. It measures the ocean below the surface, down to 500 m. The subsurface is where an El Nino is charged before it shows on top. Without these buoys the warm water volume - the fuel gauge on this panel - would not exist. NOAA PMEL

units.title: UAH satellite record
units.text: UAH satellite record The University of Alabama in Huntsville processes microwave sounder data into monthly temperatures of four atmospheric layers, from the lower troposphere to the lower stratosphere, since December 1978. Thermometers hang near the ground; satellites weigh the whole air column. That is how we see the event climb through the atmosphere with a delay of months. UAH v6.1

units.title: IRI
units.text: IRI The International Research Institute for Climate and Society at Columbia University. Every month it collects the ENSO forecasts of two dozen modelling centres into one figure - the plume. It is the only place where all the models are shown side by side on one scale. We read that figure and check every model against what the ocean actually did. IRI/CCSR Columbia University

units.title: ERSST
units.text: ERSST Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature - the monthly reconstruction of ocean temperature back to 1854, on which the official ONI is computed. It is what makes today comparable with 1877: the same method applied to ships' buckets, buoys and satellites alike. NOAA ERSST v6

units.title: FAO GIEWS
units.text: FAO GIEWS The Global Information and Early Warning System on food and agriculture at the FAO. It watches harvests and food prices country by country and issues alerts. The regional impacts on this panel lean on its alerts: it is the body that says out loud when a harvest is in trouble. FAO GIEWS

units.title: RONI, the relative ONI
units.text: RONI, the relative ONI The ONI minus the mean sea-surface anomaly of the whole tropics, 20°S–20°N, over the same three months. NOAA CPC has classified El Niño and La Niña by it since February 2026. When the whole tropical ocean is warm, the plain ONI overstates how hard the atmosphere is being pushed; the atmosphere answers to the contrast, not to the absolute. The gap between ONI and RONI is the warm background this event runs on. NOAA CPC, RONI.ascii.txt; L'Heureux et al. 2024

units.title: Westerly wind burst
units.text: Westerly wind burst A week or so of westerly wind anomalies over the western equatorial Pacific, where the trade winds normally blow from the east. Here: at least two sigma above normal for five days or longer, averaged over six points between 130°E and 180°. A burst pushes warm water down and east as a Kelvin wave; two to three months later that water surfaces off South America and the event steps up. Bursts are how an El Niño is fed. ERA5 10 m wind via Open-Meteo; TAO moorings for the check

units.title: Madden–Julian Oscillation
units.text: Madden–Julian Oscillation A pulse of cloud and wind that travels east around the tropics every 30–60 days. Its position is given as one of eight phases; its strength as an amplitude, with 1 the line between organised and not. Phases 6–8 put the pulse's westerlies over the western Pacific, and that is when wind bursts cluster. The MJO does not cause an El Niño, but it times the pushes. NOAA PSL OMI index (Kiladis et al. 2014)

units.title: Indian Ocean Dipole
units.text: Indian Ocean Dipole The sea-surface temperature of the western tropical Indian Ocean minus the eastern; the Dipole Mode Index, DMI. Positive means a warm west and a cool east off Sumatra. A positive dipole with an El Niño is the classic recipe for a weak Indian monsoon and a dry southern Australian autumn, and for a wet East Africa. For the Gulf it is the second index after ENSO for winter rain. HadISST via NOAA PSL, monthly since 1870

units.title: Depth of the 20 °C isotherm
units.text: Depth of the 20 °C isotherm How deep you have to go before the water is colder than 20 °C. A stand-in for the thermocline, the boundary between the warm surface layer and the cold deep. It needs no climatology: in the eastern Pacific it is normally shallow, and when the warm layer arrives with a Kelvin wave it deepens by tens of metres. That is the event seen from below. TAO/TRITON moorings, our interpolation

units.title: TAO/TRITON moorings
units.text: TAO/TRITON moorings A line of buoys across the equatorial Pacific, run by NOAA PMEL and JAMSTEC, measuring temperature at a dozen depths, wind and currents every day since the 1980s. They are the raw measurement under the surface: satellites see the skin, the moorings see the heat that has not surfaced yet. Each mooring's anomaly here is against its own thirty-year record. NOAA PMEL via CoastWatch ERDDAP

units.title: GODAS
units.text: GODAS NCEP's Global Ocean Data Assimilation System: a reanalysis that blends moorings, floats and satellites into a continuous three-dimensional field of the ocean, monthly, on a 1° by ⅓° grid with 40 depth levels. It fills the gaps between the moorings and gives the equatorial section as one picture. It lags about six weeks and smooths extremes; the moorings are the check on it. NCEP via NOAA PSL OPeNDAP

units.title: Ocean heat content
units.text: Ocean heat content The heat stored in the upper ocean, 0–700 m or 0–2000 m, as an anomaly from the 1955–2006 mean, in units of 10²² joules. NOAA NCEI computes it from Argo floats and ship data every three months. It is the reservoir the event draws on. A record reservoir means the statistical models, trained on a cooler ocean, are reading a different system than the one they learned. NOAA NCEI, 3-monthly

units.title: Earth's energy imbalance
units.text: Earth's energy imbalance The difference between the sunlight the planet absorbs and the heat it radiates back, measured from satellites (CERES). Positive means the planet is gaining heat. It more than doubled in two decades and was at a record in 2025 — about twice what the CMIP6 models expected. Quoted from the literature here, not measured by us: the CERES series sits behind an ordering tool. Mauritsen et al., AGU Advances 2025; NASA CERES

units.title: Multivariate ENSO Index
units.text: Multivariate ENSO Index One index built from five fields together: sea-level pressure, surface wind, sea and air temperature, and cloudiness over the tropical Pacific. Bimonthly, in standard deviations. An independent check on our three-sign coupling score: if MEI is high the ocean and the atmosphere are moving together, whatever any single index says. NOAA PSL, MEI v2

units.title: OISST NRT
units.text: OISST NRT The preliminary version of NOAA's daily quarter-degree sea-surface temperature grid, available one day behind; the final version follows about two weeks later and revises the last days by a few hundredths. It is why the daily Niño boxes on this panel are one day old rather than three weeks. The spliced days are marked preliminary and re-pulled every update until the final values arrive. NOAA NCEI via CoastWatch ERDDAP

units.title: Persian Gulf box
units.text: Persian Gulf box The sea between 24–30°N and 48–56°E on the same NOAA grid, averaged over sea cells only, with its own 1991–2020 climatology. Above about 35 °C desalination intakes, coral and fisheries are under stress; the Gulf is shallow and heats fast. It is the one El Niño-adjacent number on this panel that is measured at Kuwait's coast. NOAA OISST NRT via ERDDAP, our box mean

units.title: Food-security weight
units.text: Food-security weight A hand-set score from 1 to 5 for each commodity in the price table: 5 for the staples that carry about a fifth of the world's calories each (wheat, rice), 4 for sugar, maize and palm oil, 3 for soybean oil and the fertilisers that set the next sowing, 2 for fish meal (feed), 1 for niche and income crops (coconut oil, coffee, cocoa). The basis is the share of world dietary energy in the FAO food balance sheets and the place in the food chain. A 30 % move in wheat and a 30 % move in coconut oil are not the same news. The weight orders the table and the alerts: a large yearly move in a staple raises an alert, the same move in a niche crop only shows in the table. FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets; our own scoring in tools/enso/air.py (FOOD_WEIGHT)

units.title: Fresh, not yet assessed
units.text: Fresh, not yet assessed Data that arrived after the last assessment. A light run pulls every source and applies the same rules, but does not call the model, write a snapshot or touch the verdict; its result is kept apart as the fresh layer and drawn with a hollow pulsing dot. Sources move daily, assessments every few days. The fresh layer shows what has come in since, and its triggers say whether it deserves a new assessment: a new record or SHOUT, a daily value outside the assessed forecast band, a new weekly or monthly release, a changed risk level, the risk index moving by three points or more. tools/enso/fresh.py (thresholds at the top of the file); the Ops tab lists the triggers

units.title: Runs and sources
units.text: Runs and sources The service register of the panel: every run (full update, light run, links, mooring records, publish, review mark) with its start, duration and outcome, and every source with its date range, last update and any error. Written at the end of each run, not live. It answers the question a maintainer asks first: what ran, when, did it finish, and which source is behind. tools/enso/ops.py → data/enso/ops.json and runs.json

units.title: Spectral watch
units.text: Spectral watch For each daily series the last 30 days are tested for a spectral line at 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7 days above a red-noise background (χ² test); the line is compared with every past 30-day window and with the same window of 1982, 1997, 2015 and 2023. The owner's hypothesis: a comb of short periods appears when a system reaches the edge of its stability. It is watched, not assumed; by chance one or two 99 % lines are always present among two dozen series, so a signal needs 99.9 % or a comb, nine days of persistence and the top percentile of history. tools/enso/spectral.py → data/enso/spectral.json

units.title: Land regions (ERA5 boxes)
units.text: Land regions (ERA5 boxes) Six boxes over land (northern Gulf, central Europe, Peru coast, Java, East Africa, northern India): the mean of a 3×3 grid of ERA5 points inside the box, cosine-weighted, daily since 1981, treated exactly like the global series. The impacts of El Niño land on regions; a box mean is weather averaged over a country-sized area, not a point, but it still swings more than the ocean boxes. ERA5 via Open-Meteo archive; tools/enso/regions_daily.py

units.title: Rain, ERA5 and GPCP
units.text: Rain, ERA5 and GPCP Regions: ERA5 daily precipitation summed over the box, the last 30 and 90 days against the 1991–2020 normal of the same calendar window and against every year since 1981. Planet: GPCP monthly, satellites and gauges over land and ocean, since 1979. Drought and flood are how El Niño reaches food and people. A reanalysis is biased in the tropics, so the panel shows percentages of normal, not millimetres; GPCP is the second source and the only one for the planet as a whole. Open-Meteo archive (ERA5); NOAA PSL GPCP v2.3; tools/enso/precip.py

units.title: Raw satellite granules (NOAA-21)
units.text: Raw satellite granules (NOAA-21) Level-1 radiances read straight from the NOAA-21 granules in the open NODD bucket: CrIS infrared spectra (blind under cloud, which is itself the convection signal) and ATMS microwave brightness temperatures (through cloud), two boxes, day and night, the window 1 July to 6 September of 2023–2026. Schema v2 keeps a histogram of the window brightness temperature per day, so cloud floors, clear-sky shares and the window-trap indices G and G_clear are computed without re-reading the granules; AIRS on Aqua is being collected as a second, independent satellite. The first measurement on this panel made by us from raw data rather than taken as somebody's product. Everything called temperature there is brightness temperature; the base starts in February 2023, so the sigmas are short. external collector C:\CL\radiance (its author updates it); data/enso/radiance.json

units.title: Raw Walker contrast
units.text: Raw Walker contrast Brightness temperature at 900 cm⁻¹ over the Niño 3.4 box minus the same over the warm pool, in kelvin, from the raw CrIS granules. In a normal year the east is 19–26 K warmer at the top of the atmosphere because the west is under deep cloud. A fall to zero means the deep convection has moved east: the Walker circulation has collapsed or reversed, which is the atmospheric half of a strong El Niño. data/enso/radiance.json, formula in meta.formulas

units.title: Hovmöller diagram
units.text: Hovmöller diagram Time runs down the page, longitude across; each row is one month of the subsurface anomaly along the equator from the GODAS reanalysis, at about 95 m or as the depth of the 20 °C isotherm. A Kelvin wave shows as a warm band sliding from west to east over two to three months; the diagram is the standard way to see the heat move, and the past strong events sit beside it on the same calendar months. GODAS via NOAA PSL; tools/enso/subsurface.py --hov

units.title: Mentions feed
units.text: Mentions feed Headlines from the Google News editions in nine languages and Bing News, deduplicated; Wikipedia page views of the El Niño article in nine languages; the posts of agencies and forecast centres that mention ENSO. Talk about the event, not a measurement of it: how much attention it gets, where, and what the centres say. Headlines are shown as written by the publishers. tools/enso/mentions.py → data/enso/mentions.json

units.title: GPCP
units.text: GPCP The Global Precipitation Climatology Project monthly product: satellites and rain gauges merged on a 2.5° grid over land and ocean since 1979, in millimetres per day. The only long series that says whether the planet as a whole received more or less rain; used here for the planet and as a second source beside ERA5 for the land boxes. NOAA PSL, precip.mon.mean.nc

units.title: Cloud floors
units.text: Cloud floors Each satellite scene sorted by the brightness temperature of the 11 µm window: deep convection below 235 K, mid cloud 235–270 K, low cloud 270–285 K, clear when the window reads within 4 K of the sea surface. Shares of scenes per day, from the raw CrIS granules. The day-time cloud share is the panel's proxy for albedo: more reflecting cover over the east Pacific, less over the west. Infrared does not measure albedo itself; VIIRS would. external collector C:\CL\radiance, schema v2; data/enso/radiance.json → clouds

units.title: G and G_clear, window trap
units.text: G and G_clear, window trap G = sea surface temperature (OISST, K) minus the mean 11 µm brightness temperature over the box: how much the atmosphere closes the thermal window. G_clear is the same on the warmest tenth of scenes only, i.e. the least cloudy ones. The full G follows cloud, not greenhouse gases. G_clear is the proxy for the greenhouse action of water vapour; on the strictest 1 % of scenes the 2026 signal over Niño 3.4 halves to +1.4 K but stays. Over the warm pool there are almost no truly clear scenes, so its G_clear is an upper bound, not a measurement. external collector C:\CL\radiance, schema v2; data/enso/radiance.json → greenhouse, greenhouse_clear

units.title: Regime watch
units.text: Regime watch Watching the link between sea temperature and the response of the air, instead of watching the readings themselves. One point per year, a line fitted through the logarithm of the share of deep convection, and the question is whether the line itself moves. A record is a position on a curve; a change of regime is the curve bending. This is the only block on the panel that watches the curve. computed by the radiance collector, block regime

units.title: Extrapolation
units.text: Extrapolation Reading a fitted relation outside the range of values it was fitted on. The line still draws, but the data can no longer say what shape it has out there, and a bend too small to see statistically can flip the answer. This year's sea is warmer than any year the convection link was fitted on, so where the link puts this year is a statement about the shape of the curve, not a measurement. The panel says so rather than printing the number as a reading. stated by the radiance collector in its own caveats

units.title: How far past its own threshold
units.text: How far past its own threshold For a risk that has a numeric rule, the share of the way from the threshold that granted its level to the next threshold, 0 to 1. Written only when both ends already exist as real quantities: the next level's threshold, a natural hundred per cent, a full count, or the series' own historical maximum. Levels are coarse: most rules set a constant, so risks inside one level looked identical. This says which of them is only just over the line and which has run far past it. It is not a measure of danger, and where no honest ceiling exists it is left empty rather than invented. computed in tools/enso/watch.py, air.py, subsurface.py

units.title: Forecast against fact
units.text: Forecast against fact The average size of the miss between a weather forecast issued N days earlier and what the reanalysis later recorded, per city, per parameter, per lead time. Bias is the same miss with its sign kept, so a steady over- or under-forecast shows up as a number rather than cancelling out. A local, faster version of the same question the model plume asks about the ocean: how well is the system being predicted right now. When the misses grow together across cities, the atmosphere is doing something the models were not built on. Open-Meteo forecasts against ERA5, computed by us in tools/enso/cities.py

units.title: melt energy (positive degree-days)
units.text: melt energy (positive degree-days) The sum of daily mean temperatures above freezing over a year, in °C·day. A day at +5 °C adds five, a day at −3 adds nothing. Ice does not care how warm the warmest day was; it cares how much heat crossed it in total. This sum is the standard melt index of glaciology and feeds the degree-day models used to turn weather into meltwater. We use it instead of counting days above zero because that count saturates: high in the Alps every summer day is already above freezing, so a record-hot year looks ordinary by day count and shows up plainly here. our own calculation from ERA5-Land daily means

units.title: phase
units.text: The rest of the panel measures how big this event is. This page asks whether the rules themselves are still holding. A record is a position on the curve; a change of regime is the curve giving way. The reading is a judgement, not a measurement, and the rule that produced it is printed next to it. Three long records of the index itself (PSL monthly Ni\u00f1o 3.4 since 1948, NOAA CPC ONI since 1950, NOAA CPC weekly since 1981), the sea-to-air relation fitted by the satellite radiance collector on twenty-odd years of CrIS and AIRS, the three coupling signs from our own daily series, and NOAA warm water volume. The arithmetic is ours. Memory is the lag-1 autocorrelation of each record inside a sliding window, after removing the seasonal cycle by month-of-year means and a slow component by a Gaussian filter; the trend across windows is a Kendall tau, reported both over the whole record and over its last third, with the count of non-overlapping windows beside it because overlapping windows inflate significance. units.title: verdict
units.text: This is the machine’s summary of where the event stands today, in plain words: what is happening, whether it has turned, what to watch next and what we are not sure about. A second machine checks every number in it before it goes out. The verdict is written by DeepSeek V4 Pro from the numbers on this panel and checked by Claude (Fable) against the same numbers; nothing in it is typed by hand. The numbers come from the daily and weekly rows below. The model receives a digest of the panel’s state (series, ranks, records, detectors, model plume) and returns verdict, turning point, outlook, watch list, confidence and caveats; a review pass compares each number with the digest and edits wording only. Corrections to earlier verdicts stay in the history.

units.title: overview
units.text: One screen with everything: the key numbers on top, and below them small versions of every chart. Point at a tile to read what it means, click it to open the full scene. Every tile is the same chart as on its own scene, drawn small from the same files; the strip on top repeats the headline numbers. Tiles are rendered by the scene chart functions in a tight mode: annotations removed, axes thinned to first and last labels, viewBox cropped to the drawn content. The strip is built from latest.json, precip.json, radiance.json, spectral.json and mentions.json.

units.title: news
units.text: What changed in the last week and what is due next: new records, alerts that fired, risks that moved a level, and the releases we are waiting for. Built by rules from the value journal (data/enso/journal.json): a line appears when a number, a risk level, an alert or the verdict changed in the last seven days. Release dates come from each source’s schedule. Unchanged values are skipped; absolute series carry no sign; a verdict rewritten on the same numbers is marked as reworded, not changed. Nothing here is written by a model.

units.title: mentions
units.text: How much the world is talking about the event and where: headlines by language, Wikipedia readers per day, and what the forecast centres publish. This is talk, not measurement. Google News RSS editions in nine languages and Bing News (headlines and publisher), Wikimedia page views of the El Niño article in nine languages, RSS of agencies and forecast centres filtered to ENSO posts. Each edition holds only its latest hundred items, so older days are undercounted; duplicates are removed by normalised title; GDELT is optional and rate-limited; official feeds show only posts mentioning ENSO and list the silent ones.

units.title: now
units.text: Where the event stands against the strongest ones on record on the same calendar days, week by week and on the map of the Pacific. A rank of 1 means warmer than any past event at this point of the year. NOAA CPC weekly Niño indices (wksst9120), NOAA OISST v2.1 daily boxes read from the ERDDAP grid with our own 1991–2020 climatologies, NOAA ONI, IRI plume, Natural Earth coastline. Analogue years are 1982, 1997, 2015 and 2023 aligned on day of year; the map colours the four Niño boxes by the weekly anomaly and shows the same week of the comparison event underneath; the play control steps the last twenty weeks.

units.title: ocean
units.text: The ocean from the surface down: daily surface temperature by box, the moorings that measure the warm water below, and the reanalysis picture of heat moving east along the equator month by month. OISST v2.1 daily boxes (own climatology), TAO/TRITON moorings via PMEL ERDDAP (daily profiles), GODAS reanalysis via NOAA PSL OPeNDAP (monthly sections and the Hovmöller diagram). Mooring anomalies are against the 1991–2020 climatology of each station; the SHOUT rule for the subsurface fires only above the mooring’s own record before this event; GODAS lags about six weeks and smooths extremes; the Hovmöller rows are monthly anomalies at ~95 m or the 20 °C isotherm depth.

units.title: radiance
units.text: What the satellite itself sees over the Pacific: where the tall storm clouds are, how the east-west contrast has collapsed, and how much the moist air traps heat. Measured by us from the raw data, not taken from anyone’s product. NOAA-21 CrIS and ATMS granules read straight from the anonymous NOAA NODD bucket by an external collector (C:\\CL\\radiance, schema v2); USGS catalogue; GFZ solar indices. Brightness temperatures, not air or ocean temperature; the record starts in February 2023; infrared is blind under cloud (that is the convection signal), microwave sees through; G_clear on the warmest tenth of scenes is partly residual cloud, on the strictest percent the signal halves but stays.

units.title: models
units.text: What the forecast centres expect and how well they have kept up: which models have fallen below reality, how each issue revised upward, and where the combined forecast now puts the peak. IRI/CPC ENSO plume, monthly issues: two dozen dynamical and statistical models; our classification of each model against the observed ONI. A model is counted broken when its forecast for a season already observed lies below the observed ONI by the threshold; the stack shows three issues on the same calendar; the breakdown is the share of models below reality per issue; RONI removes the warm background from ONI.

units.title: air
units.text: The atmosphere and the fuel: whether the winds and pressure have joined the ocean, how much warm water is stored below the surface to feed the event, and how the air and food prices answer. NOAA PSL daily and monthly indices (SOI, OLR, 850 hPa zonal wind), ERA5 wind via Open-Meteo, PMEL warm water volume and 300 m temperature, UAH satellite layers, World Bank Pink Sheet commodity prices. Coupling counts the atmospheric signs in place (SOI, OLR, westerlies); the fuel is warm water volume as a share of its record with its lead on the surface; layers are UAH lower-troposphere anomalies; commodity alerts use weights, seasonal z-scores and year-on-year percentiles.

units.title: trend
units.text: The daily temperature rows over the last year and more, with every past year as a band behind them, records marked, a two-week outlook from similar days, plus rain by region and a watch for unusual rhythms in the data. Daily series from climatereanalyzer.org (OISST Niño 3.4 and world ocean, ERA5 2 m air), ERA5 land boxes via Open-Meteo, GPCP monthly rain, NOAA OHC, our own spectral test and risk index history. Records are per calendar day since the start of each series; CUSUM accumulates excess above a threshold; the 14-day forecast is the spread of what followed similar states; land boxes are 3×3 ERA5 grid means; the spectral watch tests 30-day windows for lines at 2–7 days against red noise with a multiplicity correction.

units.title: regions
units.text: What this event usually does to each region and what is measured there now: the air over the region, the rain against normal, and the typical picture by season. A hand-written reference by region (typical impacts by season, food exposure, sources with DOIs), the Gulf block with measured series, and for six regions the ERA5 box series and rain from the same data as on Dynamics. Levels by scenario come from the reference tables keyed to event strength; measured blocks are shown only where a box or station exists; Gulf sea and weather series are our own OISST box and ERA5 point.

units.title: food
units.text: What food prices are doing: the world index, twelve commodities by name in dollars per tonne, and how each moved after the start of past events. A rise in time with the event is not proof of cause. FAO Food Price Index monthly, World Bank Pink Sheet monthly commodity prices, FAOSTAT dietary shares for the weights, our own onset dates for past events. Paths after onset are percentages of the onset-month price; in dollars they are scaled through the onset or today’s price; weights 1–5 order the alerts; the bundle uses a log scale; series are nominal, not inflation-adjusted.

units.title: planet
units.text: The long record behind the event: gases in the air, ice at both poles, the planet’s temperature and sea level, decades at a glance. The El Niño years and the years after them are highlighted. NOAA GML greenhouse gases, NSIDC sea ice index v4, Met Office HadCRUT5 (global) and CRUTEM5 (land), NOAA NCEI land monthly, NOAA STAR sea level, and the daily ERA5 and OISST series from climatereanalyzer (world, hemispheres, tropics, Arctic, Antarctic, ocean) drawn year by year. Annual and daily series are shown against their own baselines as stated on each chart; CO₂ uses the trend column of the GML file; sea level has no glacial isostatic adjustment.

units.title: how
units.text: The dictionary of the panel: what each term means, why it matters here, and where it comes from; plus how the whole thing is put together and when each source updates. Written by hand: glossary, method notes and the release calendar of every source. Glossary keys match data-term attributes in the code; the calendar is the publishing cadence of each provider, not our run times.

units.title: brief
units.text: One page to start from: what is happening, in plain words, and where on the panel each number lives. Written by hand from the panel’s own numbers: the NOAA weekly and official indices, the value journal, the risks and alerts, the statistics layer, the model plume, the release calendar and the regional reference. Prose is fixed text with live slots; every figure is read at render time from latest.json, journal.json and stats.json, so the page cannot drift from the data. No model is involved.

units.title: research
units.text: A conversation that builds a small research board: what you ask, the panel answers with its own statements, and the left side collects the numbers, concepts, scenes and papers involved. The statements of this panel (risks, alerts, indicators, glossary, scenes, the concept register) searched in the browser; the model contour is specified in the concept note and not yet wired. Retrieval is lexical over ~450 short units built from latest.json, journal.json, glossary.json, SCENE_INFO and concepts.json; anchors of the hits drive concepts (concepts.json) and works (links.json); saving is localStorage (b42_research).

units.title: refs
units.text: Everything we lean on: the papers we have read that support a claim, the data providers, the reports we quote, and similar projects elsewhere. Our parsed arXiv works attached to claims by a model with a deny list, the register of data sources, quoted literature, and a hand-written list of kindred projects with licences checked at the source. Links are proposed by a model from the pool of parsed works and filtered by links-deny.json; anchors are risks, alerts, regions, terms and hand-written claim blocks; a work standing at many anchors is flagged in the check as possibly too general.

units.title: chain
units.text: How a number travels: from the provider through our collectors and rules to the page you are reading. Click a node to see what depends on it. A hand-written map of sources, collectors, computed states and outputs; dates and freshness dots come from latest.json and the value journal. Nodes carry src_keys and journal keys; the green dot means the source answered on the last run; the date is when its data last changed, not when we asked.

units.title: ops
units.text: The service room: which runs happened, how long they took and whether they finished, which source is behind, and what new data has arrived that the verdict has not looked at yet. data/enso/ops.json and runs.json, written at the end of every run by ops.py; the fresh layer from fresh.py. Runs are recorded by kind with start, seconds, status and notes; sources carry date ranges read from the raw copies; the fresh layer compares light-run tails with the assessed state and lists crossed triggers.

units.title: about
units.text: What this panel is, who writes what, and how to read it. Written by hand. The division of labour: rules compute, DeepSeek writes the verdict, Claude checks it, a person runs the updates and publishes.

units.title: Verdict today
units.text: ALERT: Niño 3 is above anything measured: the warm patch off South America reached +3.7 °C, exceeding +3.3 °C, the highest before this event began (1997-11-12). Niño 3.4 (the patch by which El Niño is judged) is at +2.96 °C and above all analogues for these dates, so the event is still strengthening. Niño 3.4 14-day change turns negative (now +0.351 °C total). CUSUM falls from 147.12 toward its 5.0 threshold. The 30-day record run breaks (a day not the warmest for that calendar day since 1982). The active westerly wind burst ends: its peak of 6.46 m/s falls below the 4.11 m/s threshold. The warm pool at 100 m under 125°W falls from +11.3 °C.

units.title: Gulf and Arabian Peninsula
units.text: Gulf and Arabian Peninsula UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Yemen The Gulf states import 80–90 % of their food and grow almost no cereals: the exposure is entirely to world prices, shipping and the harvests of exporters. Yemen combines that dependence with an ongoing food emergency. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins. Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

units.title: East Africa
units.text: East Africa Kenya, Somalia, southern Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda Large food-insecure population; cereal imports are 20–40 % of consumption in Kenya and Somalia; floods hit pastoral and lowland cropping areas hardest. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins. Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

units.title: Southern Africa
units.text: Southern Africa Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Botswana, Namibia Maize-dependent diets and thin reserves; Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia declared drought emergencies in 2024. Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early. Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

units.title: Pacific Islands
units.text: Pacific Islands Fiji, Papua New Guinea highlands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Micronesia Small islands import most staples and depend on shipping; the 1997-98 event brought famine conditions to the PNG highlands. Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early. Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

units.title: Central America and the Caribbean
units.text: Central America and the Caribbean Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Haiti, Cuba, Dominican Republic Haiti and the dry-corridor countries combine high import dependence with chronic food insecurity and out-migration. Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early. Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

units.title: Southeast Asia and Indonesia
units.text: Southeast Asia and Indonesia Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea Rice self-sufficiency is thin in Indonesia and the Philippines, and both import in El Niño years; Thailand and Vietnam are exporters whose smaller crops raise world prices. Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

units.title: Peru, Ecuador and the Andes
units.text: Peru, Ecuador and the Andes Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Colombia Peru imports wheat and maize; fishmeal exports and coastal agriculture (rice, mango, asparagus) are hit directly, and Colombia and Bolivia rely on imported wheat. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins. Prepare for a collapse of coastal upwelling fisheries: fishing bans, income support, alternative supply of fish protein.

units.title: Sahel
units.text: Sahel Mali, Niger, Chad, Burkina Faso, Senegal, Sudan The highest structural food insecurity, conflict, and cereal imports of 30–60 % of consumption in Mauritania and Senegal; any price shock becomes a crisis. Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early. Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

units.title: North Africa and the Levant
units.text: North Africa and the Levant Egypt, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran The world's largest wheat importers: Egypt, Algeria and Morocco import 50–75 % of their cereals, and Lebanon and Jordan more. Exposure runs through world prices and the harvests of the Black Sea exporters. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins. Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.

units.title: South Asia
units.text: South Asia India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal Largely self-sufficient in cereals but with a huge population close to the margin; India restricts exports in bad years, and that alone moves world rice prices. Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

units.title: East Asia
units.text: East Asia China, Japan, Korea China holds large reserves but is the largest soybean and a major maize importer; Japan and Korea import most of their cereals but are wealthy enough to secure them. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

units.title: Southern Cone
units.text: Southern Cone southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, northern Argentina; north-east Brazil Net exporters of soybean, maize and wheat: the world-price effect is usually favourable because the crops are bigger, and the local risk is floods and the north-eastern drought. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

units.title: Australia and New Zealand
units.text: Australia and New Zealand eastern and northern Australia, New Zealand A major wheat exporter: a poor Australian crop tightens the world wheat balance and raises prices for importers elsewhere. Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.

units.title: North America
units.text: North America United States, Canada, northern Mexico The largest maize and soybean exporter; El Niño winters are usually favourable for US crops, which eases world supply. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

units.title: West Africa (Gulf of Guinea)
units.text: West Africa (Gulf of Guinea) Nigeria, Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon Rice and wheat imports matter (Nigeria, Ghana); the exposure runs through world prices rather than local weather. No strong signal: watch the neighbours' harvests and world prices rather than local weather.

units.title: Europe
units.text: Europe Western, Southern and Northern Europe A net exporter of cereals overall and wealthy enough to outbid others on the world market; the risk here is price, not availability. A poor southern-European harvest raises world prices for the importers elsewhere. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.

units.title: Russia and Central Asia
units.text: Russia and Central Asia European Russia, Siberia, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan Russia and Kazakhstan are among the largest wheat exporters: what matters for the world is their harvest, not their imports. A poor Black Sea crop is the single fastest route from weather to global bread prices. Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
